title: Isolation classes and graceful deprioritization for Dedicated capacity
creator: Nora Patel
description:
Background: As Dedicated customers run mixed-tenancy workloads on reserved pools we continue to see unpredictable tail latency and hard failures during transient demand spikes. Current eviction and burst flows are either too aggressive (causing visible SLA violations) or too permissive (allowing noisy tenants to consume buffer capacity).

This PRD defines 'isolation classes' (tiered isolation + deprioritization) and a graceful preemption window to achieve predictable tenant-level SLAs while preserving capacity utilization. The goal is both an API/serving change and console + observability surfaces so operators can configure, monitor, and roll out policies safely.

Goals:
- Introduce isolation classes that map tenants to behavioral QoS profiles (Strict, Standard, Elastic).
- Provide a graceful deprioritization/preemption flow: autoscale buffer -> deprioritize non-critical requests -> short preemption window -> soft-evict only if necessary.
- Expose controls in Console and via API for project owners and Redwood operators to set class, budget, and preemption policy.
- Make behavior auditable (events, logs, and dashboard metrics) and testable in a canary before cluster-wide rollout.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not change billing or billing models.
- It does not implement model-level token-rate shaping (separate follow-up).
requirements: R1: Define three isolation classes and their defaults: Strict (no preemption, dedicated min capacity), Standard (background deprioritization with 30s preemption window), Elastic (aggressive deprioritization, 5s preemption window).
R2: API: PUT /tenants/{id}/isolation-class with fields: class, min_reserved, burst_budget, preemption_behavior, deprioritization_policy.
R3: Serving runtime: implement request priority tagging, deprioritization queues, and a preemption scheduler that respects tenant min_reserved and burst_budget.
R4: Console: tenant settings page to view and edit isolation class, show projected impact and simulated preemption for a chosen window.

R5: Observability: emit events for state transitions (deprioritized, preemption-window-start, preempted, soft-evicted) and surface per-tenant metrics: deprioritization_rate, preemption_count, tail_latency_p95/p99, and failed_requests_due_to_eviction.
R6: Safety: add cluster-level guardrails to avoid global mass-evictions (max_eviction_rate per minute per pool) and an operator kill-switch to pause preemption flows.
R7: Backwards compatibility: default new tenants to 'Standard' and ensure no change to behavior for tenants that do not opt-in.
R8: Acceptance tests and canary plan: synthetic load tests that demonstrate expected latency degradation curves and rollback conditions.
R9: Documentation: API docs, Console help text, runbook for oncall with playbook steps for investigating preemption incidents.
R10: Accessibility: Console UI changes must meet existing company UI accessibility baseline.
acceptance_criteria: AC1: Three isolation classes exist in API and Console; creating/updating a tenant's class returns 200 and reflects in the UI within 30s.

AC2: Under controlled synthetic spike (test harness), Strict tenants maintain >= 99.9% of baseline p95 latency; Standard tenants show a configurable, documented p95 degradation threshold; Elastic tenants may be deprioritized but must degrade gracefully without immediate hard failures.

AC3: Preemption events are emitted as structured logs and shown in Console events within 60s of transition; each event includes tenant_id, pool_id, class, reason, and a link to supporting trace/trace_id.

AC4: Guardrail enforcements (max_eviction_rate) prevent more than X% of active tenants in a pool from being evicted in a 5-minute window; test harness validates guardrail triggers and operator kill-switch stops further preemptions.

AC5: Integration tests exercise the PUT tenant API, the runtime deprioritization queue, and the preemption scheduler in CI; end-to-end tests included in staging pass consistently for three consecutive runs before canary start.
AC6: Console shows projected SLA impact when changing class; UX copy approved by Design and PM; accessibility audit passed and documented.

AC7: Rollout canary executed against 3 dedicated pools with success criteria met (no customer-facing incident, telemetry within thresholds) before enabling cluster-wide; rollback procedure documented, exercised, and validated.
AC8: Runbook added and reviewed by SRE and support; at least two oncall drills executed using staging incidents prior to GA.
AC9: No changes to billing or quotas; acceptance tests confirm cost meters unchanged by default for Standard-class tenants.
AC10: Stakeholder sign-off from PM, ENG (runtime + orchestration), Design, SRE, and Legal for audit logging retention policy.
success_metrics: SM1: Reduce pool-level hard-evictions by 80% during transient spikes compared to baseline (30d window).
SM2: Maintain 99.9% availability for Strict-class tenants over first 90 days post-rollout.
SM3: Decrease number of post-spike customer support tickets related to evictions by 60% within quarter.
SM4: Telemetry shows median preemption duration < configured window for Standard class in 95% of cases.
rollout_plan: Step 0: Finalize API contract and internal feature flagging design (2 weeks).
Step 1: Implement serving runtime hooks and telemetry (eng team A) + unit tests (3 weeks).
Step 2: Console UI and API surface (eng team B + Design) behind flag; integration tests in staging (2 weeks).
Step 3: Canary: enable on 3 non-critical pools (48h observation), run synthetic spike tests; if pass -> expand to 25% of pools (7 days).
Step 4: Gradual rollout with monitoring and automatic rollback triggers (30 days).
Step 5: GA and deprecation of old ad-hoc eviction scripts (announce 2 weeks prior).
